h1: The 8 Best Printers for Envelopes of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Printers for Envelopes: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 8 best printers for envelopes, comparing laser and inkjet models on tray design, duplex, and everyday mailing use.
summary: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is our top laser for steady business mailing. The Brother HL-L2405W is the budget laser pick, and the Brother HL-L3220CDW adds color for branded envelopes. For occasional invitations, the Canon PIXMA TS4320 and HP DeskJet 4355 handle envelopes alongside everyday printing.
intro: Envelope printing breaks cheap printers more than any other job. An envelope is thicker than paper and has a seam, so a printer that jams or smears on it makes you waste a stack before you find the right feed setting.

We reviewed eight printers on paper, comparing laser versus inkjet, tray and envelope feed design, and extra functions. None of the spec sheets guarantees perfect results on every envelope size, so we focus on engine type and feed design.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser
products.verdict: A compact laser all-in-one built for steady mailing.
products.description:
Brother packs black-and-white laser output, hands-free two-sided printing, a copier, a scanner, and wireless plus mobile printing into the compact DCP-L2640DW, priced at $200 to $500.

Laser toner is fused to the page with heat, which suits envelopes because it resists smearing and moisture better than inkjet. It leads the Brother HL-L2405W by adding scanning and copying.

Buy it if you mail regularly and want one machine for everything. The price is the sticking point, as it is the dearest laser in this group.
products.skipIf: You need color on the envelope.

products.name: Brother HL-L2405W Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser
products.verdict: A print-only laser with low per-page toner cost.
products.description:
The HL-L2405W is a print-only monochrome laser with wireless and mobile printing and a compact chassis. It is described as having a low per-page toner cost and sits in the $100 to $200 tier.

It costs less than the DCP-L2640DW because it drops scanning, copying, and duplex. That is a fair trade if envelopes and letters are all you print.

Buy it for home office envelopes on a budget. The caveat is no scanner.
products.idealFor: Home offices printing envelopes on a budget.
products.skipIf: You need scanning or two-sided printing.

products.name: Brother HL-L3220CDW Wireless Color Laser Printer
products.verdict: Color laser output for branded envelopes, up to 19 PPM.
products.description:
The HL-L3220CDW is a color laser printer running up to 19 pages per minute with a 250-sheet tray, automatic duplex, and wireless and mobile support. It is built for daily office use and sits in the $200 to $500 tier.

It places behind the monochrome Brothers for most readers only because color toner adds cost. For logos on return addresses it is the clear winner.

Choose it if branding matters on your mailing. The caveat is higher running cost.
products.skipIf: Black text is all you print.

products.name: Canon imageCLASS LBP6030w Monochrome Wireless Laser Printer
products.verdict: The least expensive laser here, at 19 PPM.
products.description:
The Canon imageCLASS LBP6030w is a print-only monochrome laser with 19 PPM speed, a compact wireless design, and a 1-year limited warranty. It comes in a white chassis and sits in the $50 to $100 tier.

It is the cheapest way to get laser toner here, undercutting the Brother HL-L2405W, but it lacks a stated mobile printing feature.

Get it if you want laser reliability for envelopes without extras. The caveat is the older, simpler design.
products.skipIf: You need scanning or mobile printing.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: An inkjet with a single envelope feed and an ADF.
products.description:
Canon built the TR4720 around a document feeder, with fax, mobile printing, wireless, and a tray that takes one envelope at a time. It sits in the $50 to $100 tier.

Inkjets lay down water-based ink, which can smear on some envelopes, so it ranks below the lasers. It handles envelopes occasionally alongside general document tasks.

Buy it if envelopes are a sideline. The caveat is the single envelope feed.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS4320 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A duplex inkjet that suits occasional card and invitation envelopes.
products.description:
The TS4320 prints color, two-sided, and over wireless, and its tray lists envelope support next to a built-in copier and scanner. It sits in the $50 to $100 tier.

It trails the TR4720 for business use because it lacks a document feeder, but it is a good fit for holiday cards and invitations.

Choose it for personal mailing. The caveat is inkjet smear risk on some envelopes.

products.name: HP DeskJet 4355 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: Guided envelope alignment with a 3-month Instant Ink trial.
products.description:
HP pairs the DeskJet 4355 with a 3-month Instant Ink trial, AI-capable printing features, and a tray with an envelope feed. It sits in the $50 to $100 tier.

It lands below the Canons because the spec sheet adds software features rather than extra hardware, but guided alignment can reduce wasted envelopes.

Buy it for occasional mailing with help from the app. The caveat is the ink cost over time.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS6520 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: An OLED display walks you through envelope setup.
products.description:
Canon gave the TS6520 a 1.42 inch OLED display, plus duplex, copying, scanning, and wireless color printing. It sits in the $50 to $100 tier.

It ranks last because the screen guidance is its main distinction and the spec sheet lists no specific envelope feature beyond that.

Pick it if you want on-screen prompts. The caveat is that it is a general inkjet.

whatMatters.detail: Laser toner is fused with heat, so it resists smearing and moisture. Inkjet ink is water-based and can smear on glossy or damp envelopes. Check the engine type in the title.
Some printers feed envelopes one at a time while others take a stack. A single feed is slow for volume. Look for envelope feed notes in the bullets.
Duplex prints both sides automatically, which helps for letters but is rarely needed for envelopes. Check whether it is listed if you also print documents.
Toner usually costs less per page than ink on volume. Check the per-page cost if the listing gives one.
Standard business envelopes are common, but larger ones may not feed. Check the manual's supported sizes.

faq.a: Not all. Check envelope support or an envelope feed on the listing.
Feeding envelopes without the right setting, causing jams or smears. Use the printer's envelope settings.

faq.q: Is laser worth it over inkjet?
faq.a: For regular mailing yes, since toner resists smearing.

faq.q: How do I set up envelope printing?
faq.a: Select the envelope size in your print dialog and load the envelope as the manual shows.
Use flat envelopes without bubbles and feed them one at a time if the printer has a single feed.

faq.q: Can I print on large envelopes?
faq.a: Check supported sizes in the manual before buying.

finalTake: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best printer for envelopes if you mail regularly, thanks to laser toner and a full feature set. The Brother HL-L2405W is the budget version, and an inkjet like the Canon TS4320 works for occasional cards. Start by deciding how often you mail, since that settles laser versus inkjet.
